name: The Borel–Cantelli Lemma
statement: If the probabilities of a sequence of events sum to a finite value, then almost surely only finitely many of the events occur.
statementAccent: then almost surely only finitely many of the events occur
meaning: This first lemma gives a simple sufficient condition — a convergent sum of event probabilities — for concluding that, with probability 1, all but finitely many of the events fail to happen. A companion second lemma provides a partial converse: if the events are independent and their probabilities sum to infinity, then almost surely infinitely many occur.
mechanism: The first lemma follows from countable subadditivity: the probability that infinitely many events occur is bounded above by the tail sum of probabilities from any starting index, which shrinks to zero as the convergent series is truncated further out. The second lemma uses independence and the bound 1−p ≤ e^(−p) to show the probability that none of a growing block occurs vanishes when the probabilities sum to infinity.

examples.text: If a monkey types keys independently and uniformly at random forever, the probabilities of typing any fixed finite text at successive positions sum to infinity, so the second lemma guarantees that text is typed infinitely often, almost surely.
For events with probability 1/n², the probabilities sum to π²/6 (finite), so the first lemma guarantees the event occurs for only finitely many n, almost surely.
The lemma is a standard tool in proofs of the strong law of large numbers and other almost-sure convergence results, by showing that "bad" deviation events occur only finitely often.

whyItMatters: It is a foundational tool for establishing almost-sure convergence, underlying rigorous proofs of laws of large numbers and other limit theorems, and it requires no independence assumption in its first, easier direction, making it broadly applicable.
limits: The first lemma only ever gives a zero-probability conclusion (events happen finitely often) and cannot show events happen infinitely often; the second lemma, which can, strictly requires independence of the events, which many real applications lack.
misreadings: People sometimes apply the second lemma’s conclusion to non-independent events, incorrectly assuming a divergent probability sum alone guarantees infinitely many occurrences.
origin: Émile Borel proved the first lemma in his 1909 paper on countable probabilities; Francesco Paolo Cantelli proved the complementary independence direction in his 1917 paper.
namedAfter: Émile Borel and Francesco Paolo Cantelli

sources.text: Borel–Cantelli lemma, Wikipedia. — both directions of the lemma and the Borel (1909)/Cantelli (1917) origin.
